claims.text: Defect-induced local energy barriers govern nucleation and growth during the first-order magnetostructural transition in as-deposited non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type HEAs.
These defect-controlled barriers govern the magnetocaloric response.
These defect-controlled barriers govern hysteresis.
The as-deposited FeMnNiGeSi-type alloy has an ordered single-phase hexagonal structure.
The as-deposited alloy has a high density of defects, including dislocations and grain boundaries.
The as-deposited alloy undergoes a sharp, highly hysteretic, first-order magnetostructural transition.
Controlled post-deposition annealing will reduce defect density.
Controlled post-deposition annealing will alter grain-boundary characteristics.
Defect density and grain-boundary structure create local variations in nucleation barriers for the phase transformation.
Annealing-induced defect reduction will make the alloy more microstructurally homogeneous.
Microstructural homogenization will narrow the distribution of local nucleation barriers.
Narrowing the distribution of local nucleation barriers will broaden and make less abrupt the magnetostructural transition.
Annealing will reduce hysteretic losses relative to the as-deposited baseline.
Annealing will preserve a sizable magnetic entropy change.
The annealing-modified microstructure will improve effective heat exchange.
The baseline alloy has limited heat-exchange efficiency partly because of its low surface-to-volume ratio.
The predictions apply only to annealing treatments that avoid phase decomposition and excessive grain growth.
Heat treatment can reduce the distribution of magnetic exchange energies and produce a more magnetically homogeneous HEA.
Non-equiatomic HEAs can retain strong mechanical properties and can improve electrical, thermal, or magnetic properties relative to equiatomic counterparts.
Failure to obtain statistically significant transition broadening and hysteresis reduction, or an adverse entropy-change response, would refute the proposed defect-governed explanation.

contradictions.description: The baseline is said to contain many defects and local barrier variations yet to exhibit a very sharp transition, while annealing is said to homogenize and narrow those barrier variations but broaden the transition. The stated direction between barrier-distribution width and transition width is internally inconsistent.

Limited baseline heat exchange is attributed partly to low surface-to-volume ratio, but annealing does not explicitly change sample geometry or surface-to-volume ratio; the claimed heat-exchange improvement from microstructural modification therefore does not address this stated limiting cause.
